newsitem.title: KENYA: FOCUS-Kenya C.bank urges calm as shilling slides.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kenya C.bank urges calm as shilling slides.

text.p: Kenya's central bank appealed fpr calm on foreign exchange markets on Wednesday and intervened to stem the shilling's slide against the dollar as the currency came under fresh pressure.
The shilling dipped to a commercial average of 67 against the dollar compared to 64.25 at Tuesday's close, a decline of 4.28 percent, commercial dealers told Reuters.

The new losses meant the shilling has depreciated by 12.6 percent since news last Friday that the IMF had halted a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) to Kenya after a row over corruption.
Central Bank governor Micah Cheserem urged foreign exchange market participants to trade "in an orderly manner so that losses arising from the panic and speculative transactions would be minimised".
Commercial bank dealers said that after his statement the Central Bank intervened to stem the shilling's latest slide, selling at least $10 million.
"The shilling exchange rate to the U.S. dollar opened at a mean rate of 64 and rapidly depreciated to a selling rate as low as 69...the speed of depreciation is worrying," Cheserem said.

He said commercial banks reported that several importers were rushing to pay their foreign bills in order to minimise exchange losses while exporters were holding back dollars in anticipation of further shilling losses.
In a statement, Cheserem also said foreign investors in government treasury bills and stocks were in the market following the IMF move, buying foreign exchange to repatriate their investments.

"The combination of the above forces has caused the current turbulence in the foreign exchange market," Cheserem said. "The government has already committed itself to manage its expenditure within available resources."

Commercial dealers said investors were seriously alarmed at comments from President Daniel arap Moi that Kenyans would have to become self-reliant and that the IMF package was insignificant compared to Kenya's economy.
"Things are very bad. The market is very nervous," said a dealer, adding very little hard currency was on the market.
Another dealer said: "This is the first time the market has reacted to such news. It's actually moving an average of a shilling a day since the IMF announcement."
The dealers said the shilling had came under renewed pressure on Tuesday because of a shortfall in expected inflows from the coffee and tea sectors, Kenya's key commodity exports.
The shilling's lowest level to the dollar was 69.22 in October 1993. Cheserem said the central bank would intervene in the foreign exchange market "as and when justified".

On Tuesday, Moi downplayed the IMF ruling and told a rally in the tea and coffee growing regions of central Kenya that the IMF loan amounted to just $205 million, compared with Kenya's $3-billion economy.
Moi said Kenya would improve tax collection and commodity exports to meet any shortfalls arising from the IMF decision.

His cabinet urged investors to remain calm on Monday, saying Kenyan citizens should build the economy from their own meagre resources. But Kenyan executives and industrial analysts rejected the message as nonsense.

The shilling losses were expected to increase pressure on the 73-year old president, who is facing a go-slow by air traffic controllers and a national strike on Friday planned by an opposition-backed alliance pressing for political reforms.
Moi and his ruling KANU party are still widely expected to win a general election this year although the opposition has found fragile unity in their demands for constitutional reforms.
